learn: Why multi-step problems need explicit structure
Tree of Thought: search over reasoning paths
Step-back prompting and program-aided language models (PAL)
ReAct: interleaving reasoning with tool use
Test-time compute: more samples, verifiers and self-consistency
intro.why: Structured reasoning turns the same model into a much stronger problem solver for maths, logic, planning and fact-grounded questions, and underlies modern reasoning models and agents.

symbols: branching factor in a tree search

sections.title: Why reasoning needs structure
sections.plain: A model spends the same small amount of thinking per word, so it does better when it writes its steps out.
sections.body:
A Transformer performs a fixed amount of computation per generated token. Answering a multi-step problem in one token forces all steps into a single forward pass; generating intermediate tokens gives the model a scratchpad and more total computation. Errors also compound: if each step is right 95% of the time, three explicit steps succeed about 86% of the time, and implicit steps are riskier still.

Structures differ in shape: a chain (CoT), a tree with backtracking (ToT), principles first (step-back), code (PAL), tools (ReAct), and feedback loops (self-reflection). Test-time compute generalises all of these: spend more inference to get better answers.

sections.title: Chain-of-thought
sections.plain: Ask the model to show its working before giving the answer.
sections.body:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, either with few-shot examples that include worked reasoning or zero-shot with a cue such as "Let's think step by step."

Worked: "A shop has 3 boxes of 12 eggs and uses 20. How many are left?" A direct answer may skip a step (36); CoT writes 3 × 12 = 36, then 36 − 20 = 16.

Gains are large on arithmetic, symbolic and commonsense multi-step tasks, and grow with model size (small models can produce fluent but wrong chains). Costs: more output tokens and latency. Caveat: the written chain is not guaranteed to be a faithful explanation of how the model computed its answer.

sections.title: Tree of Thought
sections.plain: Explore several possible next steps, judge which look promising, and back up from dead ends.
sections.body:
Tree of Thought (ToT) treats reasoning as search. At each state the model (1) proposes several candidate thoughts, (2) evaluates states (e.g. "sure / maybe / impossible" or a score), and (3) a search algorithm (breadth-first with beam, or depth-first with backtracking) expands promising states and prunes others.

Worked: Game of 24 with {4, 7, 8, 8}. Starting 8 × 8 = 64 is a dead end; 4 + 7 = 11 → 11 − 8 = 3 → 8 × 3 = 24. Code example ex1's search explores 220 nodes to find it. ToT helps on puzzles, planning and creative tasks that need lookahead, at the cost of many more model calls.

sections.title: Step-back prompting and PAL
sections.plain: First recall the general principle; or let the model write code and have a computer do the maths.
sections.body:
Step-back prompting first asks an abstracted question ("Which principle governs this?"), then answers the original using that principle. Example: pressure when temperature doubles and volume halves → principle PV = nRT → P ∝ T/V → 4×. It helps knowledge-intensive reasoning (science, history) by retrieving the right concepts first.

Program-aided language models (PAL) have the model translate the problem into code (answer = boxes * per_box - used) and delegate computation to an interpreter (16). This removes arithmetic slips and handles large numbers or iteration. Program-of-thought is a close variant. Generated code must run in a sandbox.

sections.title: ReAct
sections.plain: Alternate between thinking and using a tool, and base the next thought on what the tool returned.
sections.body:
ReAct interleaves Thought (reasoning about what to do), Action (a tool call: search, lookup, calculator, API) and Observation (the tool result), repeating until an answer is reached.

Worked (ex2): heights of the Eiffel Tower (330 m) and Qutub Minar (73 m) are looked up, then calculate[330 − 73] → 257 m. Because facts come from observations, ReAct reduces hallucination and gives an auditable trace; reasoning in turn decides which tools to call. Failure modes: looping, wrong tool arguments, over-trusting bad observations. ReAct is the core loop of LLM agents (M13).

sections.title: Self-reflection
sections.plain: Try, check the result, write a note about what went wrong, and try again using the note.
sections.body:
Self-reflection (e.g. Reflexion, self-refine) adds a feedback loop: attempt → evaluate (tests, environment reward, or self-critique) → write a verbal reflection → retry with the reflection in context (a form of episodic memory).

Worked (ex2): avg(xs) = sum/len fails on [] with ZeroDivisionError; the reflection "handle the empty list first" leads to a passing second attempt.

Evidence shows reflection is most reliable with an external signal (unit tests, a checker, tool results). Pure self-critique can talk a model out of correct answers or miss its own mistakes, so verify rather than trust.

sections.title: Test-time compute and self-consistency
sections.plain: Spend more thinking at answer time: longer reasoning, more attempts, and a way to pick the best.
sections.body:
Test-time compute means improving answers by spending more inference: longer chains of thought, multiple samples, search (ToT), and verifiers that score candidates. Main strategies:

  • Self-consistency: sample n reasoning paths, majority-vote the final answer (42, 42, 7, 42 → 42).
  • Best-of-n with a verifier: a reward model, unit tests or checker picks the best candidate; can recover rare correct answers.
  • Long reasoning: reasoning models trained with RL (M9) produce extended internal chains; accuracy rises with the thinking budget.

In ex2 (p = 0.35, wrong answers spread over 5 values): majority vote 0.35 → 0.68 → 0.97 for n = 1, 16, 64; best-of-n with a perfect verifier reaches 1.00 by n = 16. Real verifiers are imperfect, and cost grows linearly with n, so compute is allocated per problem difficulty.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Faithfulness: a chain can look plausible yet not reflect the model's actual computation; check answers, not just reasoning style.
  • Overthinking: long reasoning on easy questions wastes tokens and can introduce errors.
  • Compute-optimal inference: a smaller model with more samples can match a larger one on some tasks.
  • Prompt-level reasoning still matters with reasoning models: clear problems and tools beat clever phrasing.

code.title: Chain-of-thought, PAL and Tree of Thought
code.explain: Writes the egg problem as explicit steps (36, then 16), solves it again by executing a generated program (PAL), and runs a depth-first Tree-of-Thought search on the Game of 24 with {4, 7, 8, 8}, finding 4 + 7 = 11, 11 − 8 = 3, 8 × 3 = 24 after exploring 220 nodes.
mistakes: Letting the model do long arithmetic in text.
code.notes: The search is exhaustive; an LLM-guided ToT would evaluate states with the model.
code.code:
"""Chain-of-thought as explicit steps, program-aided reasoning (PAL), and a Tree-of-Thought search."""
from itertools import combinations
from fractions import Fraction

# Chain-of-thought: write intermediate steps instead of jumping to the answer
steps = [("3 boxes of 12 eggs", 3 * 12), ("20 eggs used", -20)]
total = 0
for text, val in steps:
    total += val
    print(f"step: {text:20s} -> running total {total}")
print("answer:", total, "(a direct guess often skips the multiplication and says 3 x 12 = 36 or 12 - 20)")

# PAL: the model writes code; the interpreter does the arithmetic exactly
program = "boxes = 3\nper_box = 12\nused = 20\nanswer = boxes * per_box - used"
scope = {}
exec(program, {}, scope)
print("PAL program ->", scope["answer"])

# Tree of Thought on the Game of 24: each thought combines two numbers; search the tree with pruning
def solve(nums, path, stats):
    stats["nodes"] += 1
    if len(nums) == 1:
        return path if nums[0] == 24 else None
    for i, j in combinations(range(len(nums)), 2):
        a, b = nums[i], nums[j]
        rest = [nums[k] for k in range(len(nums)) if k not in (i, j)]
        cands = {(a + b, f"{a}+{b}"), (a * b, f"{a}*{b}"), (a - b, f"{a}-{b}"), (b - a, f"{b}-{a}")}
        if b != 0: cands.add((a / b, f"{a}/{b}"))
        if a != 0: cands.add((b / a, f"{b}/{a}"))
        for v, s in cands:
            if v < 0: continue                      # prune: negative intermediate results are not useful here
            r = solve(rest + [v], path + [f"{s}={v}"], stats)
            if r: return r
    return None
stats = {"nodes": 0}
sol = solve([Fraction(4), Fraction(7), Fraction(8), Fraction(8)], [], stats)
print("Tree of Thought on [4, 7, 8, 8]:", " ; ".join(sol), f"(explored {stats['nodes']} nodes)")
print("a single left-to-right chain commits to its first move; the tree can back up and try another branch")

code.title: ReAct, self-reflection and test-time compute
code.explain: Runs a Thought/Action/Observation trace with lookup and calculate tools (257 m), a two-attempt self-reflection loop driven by unit tests, and a simulation comparing majority voting with best-of-n plus a perfect verifier for p = 0.35 (0.68 vs 1.00 at n = 16).
mistakes: Breaking vote ties in favour of the right answer.
code.code:
"""A ReAct loop with a lookup tool, a self-reflection loop with unit tests, and test-time compute scaling."""
import numpy as np

facts = {"Eiffel Tower height": 330, "Qutub Minar height": 73}
trace = [("Thought", "I need both heights."), ("Action", "lookup[Eiffel Tower height]"),
         ("Thought", "Now the other one."), ("Action", "lookup[Qutub Minar height]"),
         ("Thought", "Subtract."), ("Action", "calculate[330 - 73]")]
for kind, text in trace:
    print(f"{kind}: {text}")
    if kind == "Action":
        name, arg = text.split("[", 1); arg = arg.rstrip("]")
        obs = facts[arg] if name == "lookup" else eval(arg)
        print(f"Observation: {obs}")
print("Answer: the Eiffel Tower is 257 m taller (330 m vs 73 m)")

# Self-reflection: attempt, test, reflect on the failure, retry
attempts = ["def avg(xs): return sum(xs) / len(xs)",
            "def avg(xs): return sum(xs) / len(xs) if xs else 0.0"]
tests = [([1, 2, 3], 2.0), ([], 0.0)]
for i, code in enumerate(attempts, 1):
    ns = {}; exec(code, ns)
    fails = []
    for xs, want in tests:
        try:
            if ns["avg"](xs) != want: fails.append(xs)
        except Exception as e:
            fails.append(f"{xs} raised {type(e).__name__}")
    print(f"attempt {i}: {'all tests pass' if not fails else 'failed ' + str(fails)}")
    if fails: print("  reflection: empty input divides by zero; handle the empty list first")

# Test-time compute: more samples + a verifier vs majority vote
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
p, trials = 0.35, 4000
for n in (1, 4, 16, 64):
    correct = rng.random((trials, n)) < p
    best_of_n = correct.any(axis=1).mean()                  # perfect verifier picks a correct one if any
    wrong = rng.integers(0, 5, size=(trials, n))            # wrong answers spread over 5 values
    votes = np.where(correct, 5, wrong)                     # label 5 = correct; ties break toward a wrong answer
    maj = np.mean([np.bincount(v, minlength=6).argmax() == 5 for v in votes])
    print(f"n={n:3d}: majority vote {maj:.2f}, best-of-n with a perfect verifier {best_of_n:.2f}")
print("with p = 0.35 voting still helps because errors scatter; a good verifier helps much more")
